claims.text: The starting material is an additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy.
The as-built alloy has a single-phase fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy has a controlled distribution of alloying elements.
Selective oxidation of Ti is the primary governor of degradation during prolonged elevated-temperature exposure.
Selective Ti oxidation produces a discontinuous, nonprotective Ti-rich oxide scale.
The nonprotective Ti-rich scale compromises the underlying fcc matrix.
Oxidizing and reducing exposures at 800–900 °C can be compared while holding mechanical load and thermal cycling minimal to isolate the effect of oxygen partial pressure.
Oxide-scale continuity, phase composition, and morphology mediate oxygen transport and interfacial stress.
The Ti-rich oxide regions are likely to contain rutile TiO2.
Under oxidizing conditions, oxygen preferentially reacts with Ti to form TiO2.
Discontinuous or internally porous TiO2 disrupts formation of a continuous protective Cr-rich or mixed oxide layer.
Low-oxygen or reducing conditions suppress selective Ti oxidation and alter the scale structure.
A defective Ti-rich scale accelerates oxygen ingress into the alloy.
Accelerated oxygen ingress promotes spallation and microcracking.
The proposed degradation occurs without significantly altering the fcc matrix beyond surface effects.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a porous, discontinuous TiO2-rich scale with interfacial microcracking or spallation.
Oxidizing exposure will cause greater weight change than inert exposure, appearing as weight gain unless severe spallation causes loss.
Reducing exposure will produce a more uniform or less aggressive scale than oxidizing exposure.
An inert-atmosphere heat-treated baseline will have only a very thin or continuous protective oxide without significant degradation.
The 800–900 °C range is an applicable elevated-temperature regime for this Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti alloy system.
